                                UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                            NUCLEAR REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                  BEFORE THE COMMISSION



 In the Matter of


 NEXTERA ENERGY DUANE ARNOLD, LLC                                Docket No. 50-331-LA


 (Duane Arnold Energy Center)

NRC STAFF BRIEF IN OPPOSITION TO THE PHYSICIANS FOR SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
                         IOWA APPEAL OF LBP-26-9

                                         INTRODUCTION

       In accordance with 10 C.F.R. § 2.311 (b), the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission

(NRC) Staff files this brief in opposition to the Physicians for Social Responsibility Iowa (the

Petitioner) appeal of Atomic Safety and Licensing Board Memorandum and Order LBP-26-9. In

LBP-26-9, the Board denied the Petitioner’s five contentions challenging NextEra Energy Duane

Arnold, LLC’s (NEDA) three license amendment requests submitted to the NRC to support the

restart of power operations at the Duane Arnold Energy Center (DAEC). Here, the Petitioner

appeals only the Board’s denial of Contentions 3 (restart pathway) and 5 (NEPA segmentation),

but does not identify any error of law or abuse of discretion in the Board’s decision. Moreover,

the Petitioner acknowledges that the Board correctly found that Contention 3 is not admissible

because binding Commission precedent from CLI-26-7 bars the Petitioner’s challenge. To

support its appeal of the Board’s denial of Contention 5, which alleges illegal segmentation of

environmental impacts associated with a planned nearby data center, the Petitioner both

reiterates its prior arguments and raises new, unavailing arguments, but does not demonstrate

that the Board erred or abused its discretion. To the contrary, the Board correctly held that

Contention 5 is not admissible because the NRC is not required to study the environmental
                                                    2


effects of a planned, nearby data center or include them in the environmental review for restart

of DAEC. Therefore, the Commission should deny the Petitioner’s appeal of LBP-26-9.

                                          BACKGROUND

          In 2010, the NRC issued to NEDA a renewed facility operating license for the DAEC,

which authorized the plant’s operation until February 21, 2034. 1 In August 2020, in accordance

with 10 C.F.R. § 50.82(a)(1)(i), NEDA submitted to the NRC a letter certifying that DAEC had

permanently ceased power operations. 2 The reactor was then shut down and, in accordance

with 10 C.F.R. § 50.82(a)(1)(ii), the licensee submitted to the NRC a letter certifying that all fuel

had been permanently removed from the reactor vessel and placed in the spent fuel pool as of

October 12, 2020. 3 Later, NextEra decided to pursue the restart of the DAEC rather than its

decommissioning and submitted to the NRC three license amendment requests that would, if

approved, restore the DAEC licensing basis to what it had been just prior to the permanent

cessation of operations. 4 These license amendment requests address: (1) the DAEC operating

license and technical specifications; (2) the DAEC physical security plan; and (3) the DAEC

emergency plan. 5

filed its hearing request. 7 The NRC Secretary, for the Commission, referred the hearing request

to the Atomic Safety and Licensing Board Panel. 8 The Staff and NEDA filed answers opposing

the granting of the hearing request because the proposed contentions did not satisfy the NRC’s

contention admissibility requirements. 9 The Staff agreed that the Petitioner has satisfied its

burden of demonstrating standing. 10 On August 3, 2026, the NRC staff issued the draft

Environmental Assessment (EA) and draft finding of no significant impact (FONSI) regarding the

evaluation of the reasonably foreseeable environmental effects from proposed Federal actions

related to reauthorizing power operations at DAEC for public comment. 11 The Petitioner did not

file any new or amended contentions in response to the staff’s issuance of its EA/FONSI.

                                            DISCUSSION

        On appeal, the Petitioner does not demonstrate that the Board based its decision in

LBP-26-9 to deny Contentions 3 and 5 for failure to satisfy all of the NRC’s contention

admissibility requirements on an error of law or abuse of its discretion. Therefore, the

Commission should deny the Petitioner’s appeal.

I.   The Petitioner Does Not Demonstrate a Board Error of Law or Abuse of Discretion

     A. Requirements for Appeal of a Board Order Denying a Hearing Request

        Under 10 C.F.R. § 2.311, a Board order denying a hearing request is appealable by the

petitioner on the question as to whether the hearing request should have been granted. On

threshold matters such as contention admissibility, though, the Commission will defer to the

Board’s rulings unless an appeal demonstrates an error of law or abuse of discretion. 14

Accordingly, an appeal of a Board’s contention admissibility ruling that consists of just a

“[r]ecitation of an appellant’s prior positions in a proceeding or statement of general

disagreement with a decision’s result is not sufficient.” 15 In addition, a petitioner may not, for the

first time on appeal, “present[] arguments and evidence never provided to the Board.” 16 And an

       B. Requirements for Contention Admissibility

           The requirements for contention admissibility are in 10 C.F.R. § 2.309(f)(1), which states

that a hearing request must “set forth with particularity” the contentions that the petitioner seeks

to raise and that, for each contention, six criteria must be satisfied. 18 The contention

admissibility requirements are “strict by design” and a failure to satisfy any one of the six criteria

renders a contention inadmissible. 19

       C. The Petitioner Does Not Demonstrate an Error of Law or Abuse of Discretion in the
          Board’s Denial of Contention 3

           In Contention 3, the Petitioner argued that the NRC has no authority to approve the

license amendments requested by NextEra to permit restart because there is no dedicated

regulatory procedure for restarting a closed reactor. 20 In both its Reply and at oral argument, the

Petitioner conceded that Commission precedent forecloses its challenge to the Duane Arnold

restart. 21 Despite acknowledging that its arguments were contrary to Commission precedent,

the Petitioner nonetheless asserted that it was raising the contention before the Board to

preserve the issue for judicial review. 22

           In LBP-26-9, the Board correctly found Contention 3 to be foreclosed by Commission

precedent. 23 The Board noted that all participants agreed that Contention 3 is not admissible. 24

The Board then correctly determined that Contention 3 failed to present a genuine dispute with

the license amendment requests and is therefore inadmissible. 25

           The Petitioner provides two unpersuasive justifications challenging the Board’s rejection

of Contention 3 while at the same time acknowledging a recent Commission decision on this

exact issue in a separate restart case that supports the Board’s decision here. First, the

Petitioner both asserts that it is appealing the Board’s rejection of Contention 3 to preserve the

issue for judicial review and requests the Commission “render a decision on Contention 3.” 26

Second, while acknowledging that “Commission precedent in the Commission’s decision on this

identical issue … prevented a decision finding that Contention 3 is admissible[,]” 27 the Petitioner

requests the Commission “reverse the ASLB” based on facts and arguments incorporated by

reference from its Hearing request without demonstrating that the Board erred or abused its

discretion. 28 Therefore, there is no dispute that the Board correctly denied the admission of

Contention 3.

      D. The Petitioner Does Not Demonstrate an Error of Law or Abuse of Discretion in the
         Board’s Denial of Contention 5

           In Contention 5, the Petitioner argued that the proposed restart of DAEC and the

construction of a planned nearby data center constitute one combined project that the NRC

must evaluate together under NEPA and failing to do so impermissibly segments the project. 31

The Petitioner put forward facts to establish for the purposes of contention admissibility that a

data center would be built near the facility and roughly contemporaneously with the DAEC

restart. 32

           In LBP-26-9, the Board correctly held that Petitioner’s contention is foreclosed by the

Supreme Court’s recent seminal NEPA decision in Seven County. 33 The Board correctly

explained that the NRC does not have the authority to regulate the environmental impact of data

centers and therefore is not required to evaluate the environmental impacts of the restart of

DAEC and the construction of nearby data centers as a single project. 34 Accordingly, the Board

concluded that the Petitioner failed to demonstrate that the issue raised by the contention is

the contention is not admissible. 35 The Board then provided five additional considerations

supporting its decision: (1) a ‘but for’ causal relationship between two projects does not make

the NRC responsible for the effects of a data center; (2) not analyzing the data center and the

DAEC restart as a single federal project is not impermissible segmentation under NEPA; (3) the

NRC has no authority over the data center or its environmental impacts; (4) the NRC cannot

reject the proposed action because it disapproves of a customer’s end use of the electricity; and

(5) the Petitioner did not put at issue whether studying the environmental effects of the data

center would be useful to the NRC’s decision on the proposed action. 36

           On Appeal, the Petitioner disputes each of the Board’s five ‘additional considerations’ but

does not demonstrate that the Board abused its discretion or based its decision to reject

Contention 5 on an error of law. The Petitioner first asserts that the two projects are so

interrelated and close in time and place that they form a “single, functionally integrated project”

that must be addressed together pursuant to Seven County. 37 However, the Board correctly

explained that “even when a project is interrelated and close in time and place to the project at

hand” … [that the] “[q]uestion then is whether that is a single project within the authority of the

agency in question.” 38 The Petitioner does not dispute this portion of the Board’s analysis.

Instead, the Petitioner fixates on the Board’s additional consideration that a ‘but-for’ causal

relationship is insufficient to make an agency responsible for a particular effect. 39

the Petitioner “put forth sufficient facts to establish a basis for the geographic and temporal

NRC has authority to mitigate the environmental effects of nonfederal projects by imposing

additional mitigation measures on a federal project, which the Board already considered and

consideration that NEPA’s rule of reason does not mandate the NRC study and address the

effects of a data center as a part of the NRC’s proposed agency action, 58 and the Petitioner’s

attempt to reframe its segmentation contention on appeal as a cumulative effects contention is

improper. 59 Therefore, the Petitioner does not demonstrate on appeal that the Board abused its

discretion or made any error of law in its additional considerations for rejecting Contention 5.

that none of the Petitioner’s contentions were admissible. On appeal, the Petitioner challenges

the Board’s ruling with respect to Contentions 3 and 5 but has not demonstrated an error of law

or abuse of discretion in the Board’s reasons for denying the contentions or otherwise shown

that the Petitioner’s hearing request should have been granted. Therefore, the Commission
